DAVID PAUL MORRIS/BLOOMBERG NEWS   When President Trump sits down with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday, the most dramatic national-security story in the U.S.-China relationship will be the one neither leader raises.

   The ouster of Jensen Huang from Nvidia following revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence source has rocked the world of politics and technology. It has intensified calls in Congress for tighter controls on the sale of advanced semiconductors to China and cast a harsh spotlight on the extent of Chinese intelligence-gathering within America’s most strategically important industry.

   Yet when the two leaders meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the case is unlikely to come up. As an internal policy split within his administration over export controls burst into the open , Trump struck a conciliatory tone. “We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” he told reporters Monday.

   To understand what will likely unfold in Shenzhen, I turned to Ryan Hass, a former senior national-security official in the Obama administration who recently returned from a trip to Beijing.

   “Both leaders are clear-eyed that each side conducts espionage against the other,” said Hass, now director of the Brookings Institution’s China Center. “Neither leader could say anything to the other that would dispel or diminish this reality, and they both know it.”

   The question is what happens when Trump comes home.

   The Jensen Huang affair has given fresh ammunition to forces in Washington pushing to close loopholes in current U.S. measures that have allowed Chinese companies to access chips subject to export controls through third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia . And Beijing, according to Hass, is under no illusions. 

   “Based on my recent discussions with Chinese counterparts, they view it as a question of when and how much, not whether, there will be additional export controls,” he said.

   Xi may warn Trump privately that tightening controls further risks setting off a tit-for-tat dynamic, Hass said. 

   Beijing’s leverage—and restraint.   Beijing has shown a willingness to escalate. After Trump sharply raised tariffs on Chinese goods last year, China weaponized its dominance over rare-earth minerals, restricting exports critical to everything from electric vehicles to jet fighters. But Xi is unlikely to press the point in a way that would disrupt the fragile calm both sides have worked to maintain.

   That calm is Beijing’s overriding priority, especially as Xi prepares for a major leadership reshuffle at the Communist Party’s 21st National Congress, set for late next year, where he is expected to install a new generation of loyalists in top positions. 

   “China is not pursuing any major breakthroughs or improvements in its relationship with the United States,” Hass said. “It is working to elongate the period of fragile stability in the relationship for as long as possible.” That buys China time to strengthen its position, including by developing its own versions of the technologies Washington is trying to keep out of its hands.

   Central to that effort is a concept Beijing and Washington have labeled “constructive strategic stability”—what Hass described as “a leader-level commitment to avoid confrontation and uncontrolled escalation.” The formulation remains more conceptual than concrete, he said, but it is of great value to Beijing. Xi will press Trump to reaffirm it.

   Hass said expectations should be low for major deliverables from either the bilateral meeting or the much-discussed trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Xi is expected to use his time with Trump to signal that Beijing wants no surprises, and no sudden shifts.

   The trilateral will push Xi to the outer edge of his comfort zone . “Xi rarely enters diplomatic settings where the outcome is not predetermined,” Hass said. “His staff will do their utmost to minimize space for surprise or unexpected outcomes.” 

   But with Trump and Putin across the table, there is only so much choreography that can eliminate unscripted moments. Hass said Beijing will tightly control media access to ensure Xi is presented as in command and to limit any perception that events are going off-script.

   That is perhaps the sharpest illustration of where the relationship stands. Beijing isn’t looking for a breakthrough in Shenzhen. It wants to stave off disruptions, even as the Jensen Huang case fuels pressure in Washington for tougher export controls.

   Trump and Xi may leave the summit with their fragile truce intact. But the tensions over technology and espionage will be waiting when Trump returns home.

The scandal has triggered Justice Department and potential congressional probes , compounding concerns that Huang’s lobbying to loosen chip export controls undermined U.S. national security. These events underscore Beijing’s sweeping espionage and cyber campaign to acquire Western AI and semiconductor technology.

Why Neither Trump Nor Xi Is Likely to Raise Nvidia at Their Summit
 
Plus, a former Harvard professor is recruiting Chinese-born U.S. scholars to return, amid a growing exodus of academic talent to China
 
 
Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif. DAVID PAUL MORRIS/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

When President Trump sits down with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday, the most dramatic national-security story in the U.S.-China relationship will be the one neither leader raises.

 

The ouster of Jensen Huang from Nvidia following revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence source has rocked the world of politics and technology. It has intensified calls in Congress for tighter controls on the sale of advanced semiconductors to China and cast a harsh spotlight on the extent of Chinese intelligence-gathering within America’s most strategically important industry.

 

Yet when the two leaders meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the case is unlikely to come up. As an internal policy split within his administration over export controls burst into the open, Trump struck a conciliatory tone. “We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” he told reporters Monday.

 

To understand what will likely unfold in Shenzhen, I turned to Ryan Hass, a former senior national-security official in the Obama administration who recently returned from a trip to Beijing.

 

“Both leaders are clear-eyed that each side conducts espionage against the other,” said Hass, now director of the Brookings Institution’s China Center. “Neither leader could say anything to the other that would dispel or diminish this reality, and they both know it.”

 

The question is what happens when Trump comes home.

 

The Jensen Huang affair has given fresh ammunition to forces in Washington pushing to close loopholes in current U.S. measures that have allowed Chinese companies to access chips subject to export controls through third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia. And Beijing, according to Hass, is under no illusions. 

 

“Based on my recent discussions with Chinese counterparts, they view it as a question of when and how much, not whether, there will be additional export controls,” he said.

 

Xi may warn Trump privately that tightening controls further risks setting off a tit-for-tat dynamic, Hass said. 

 

Beijing’s leverage—and restraint.

 

Beijing has shown a willingness to escalate. After Trump sharply raised tariffs on Chinese goods last year, China weaponized its dominance over rare-earth minerals, restricting exports critical to everything from electric vehicles to jet fighters. But Xi is unlikely to press the point in a way that would disrupt the fragile calm both sides have worked to maintain.

 

That calm is Beijing’s overriding priority, especially as Xi prepares for a major leadership reshuffle at the Communist Party’s 21st National Congress, set for late next year, where he is expected to install a new generation of loyalists in top positions. 

 

“China is not pursuing any major breakthroughs or improvements in its relationship with the United States,” Hass said. “It is working to elongate the period of fragile stability in the relationship for as long as possible.” That buys China time to strengthen its position, including by developing its own versions of the technologies Washington is trying to keep out of its hands.

 

Central to that effort is a concept Beijing and Washington have labeled “constructive strategic stability”—what Hass described as “a leader-level commitment to avoid confrontation and uncontrolled escalation.” The formulation remains more conceptual than concrete, he said, but it is of great value to Beijing. Xi will press Trump to reaffirm it.

 

Hass said expectations should be low for major deliverables from either the bilateral meeting or the much-discussed trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Xi is expected to use his time with Trump to signal that Beijing wants no surprises, and no sudden shifts.

 

The trilateral will push Xi to the outer edge of his comfort zone. “Xi rarely enters diplomatic settings where the outcome is not predetermined,” Hass said. “His staff will do their utmost to minimize space for surprise or unexpected outcomes.” 

 

But with Trump and Putin across the table, there is only so much choreography that can eliminate unscripted moments. Hass said Beijing will tightly control media access to ensure Xi is presented as in command and to limit any perception that events are going off-script.

 

That is perhaps the sharpest illustration of where the relationship stands. Beijing isn’t looking for a breakthrough in Shenzhen. It wants to stave off disruptions, even as the Jensen Huang case fuels pressure in Washington for tougher export controls.

 

Trump and Xi may leave the summit with their fragile truce intact. But the tensions over technology and espionage will be waiting when Trump returns home.
